title: Why Do Pilots Never Eat the Same Meal?
description:
On many airlines, the captain and the first officer are not allowed to eat the same meal. Not because of taste, because of what happened on a flight in nineteen seventy-five, when a breakfast made more than one hundred forty people sick in the air. The cockpit is full of rules and objects like that. An axe. A rope above the window. Switches hidden under red covers. Today, ten cockpit details pilots know and passengers never notice, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:18 1. The different meals
2:48 2. The captain's seat
4:20 3. The silence below ten thousand feet
5:51 4. The five second mask
7:28 5. The rope above the window
8:54 6. The axe in the cockpit
10:25 7. The heated windshield
12:02 8. The covered switches
13:33 9. The fire handles
15:02 10. The microphone above the pilots
16:39 The verdict

Sources:
- Japan Air Lines food poisoning (3 Feb 1975, 144 sick, crew ate steak, different-cook recommendation): Wikipedia, "Japan Air Lines food poisoning incident" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Air_Lines_food_poisoning_incident
- Sterile cockpit rule (FAA 1981, Eastern 212, below 10,000 ft): Wikipedia, "Sterile flight deck rule" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterile_flight_deck_rule
- Flight crew mask on with one hand within five seconds: 14 CFR 25.1447(c)(2) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/25.1447
- Oxygen use by pilots at high altitude: 14 CFR 121.333 https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/121.333
- Crash axe on airplanes with more than 19 passenger seats: Gulf News, "Why aircraft carry crash axes" https://gulfnews.com/business/aviation/why-aircraft-carry-crash-axes-cockpit-equipment-explained-after-flydubai-flight-fz1073-incident-1.500697686
- Bird strike standards (windshield 4 lb at VC, empennage 8 lb): Federal Register 2015-17404 https://regulations.justia.com/regulations/fedreg/2015/07/20/2015-17404.html
- 25-hour cockpit voice recorder standard: AVweb https://avweb.com/aviation-news/faa-25-hour-cockpit-voice-recorder-rule
